papers.title: GSH/pH Dual-Responsive Zwitterionic mRNA Nanocomplexes for Tumor-Enriched mRNA Delivery in a B16F10 Melanoma Model.
papers.abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) therapy offers a programmable route to melanoma treatment, but its translation is limited by nuclease degradation, off-target biodistribution and endolysosomal trapping. Here we report a glutathione (GSH)/pH dual-responsive mRNA nanocomplex (mRNA-NC) fabricated by one-pot in situ polymerization of N-(3-aminopropyl)methacrylamide (APMA), 1-vinylimidazole (VI), N,N'-bis(acryloyl)cystamine (BACA), and 2-methacryloyloxyethyl phosphorylcholine (MPC) on the mRNA template. At an N/P ratio of 40, the carrier reached an encapsulation efficiency of 92.7 ± 2.1% and a loading capacity of 87.4 ± 3.2 μg mg-1, forming monodisperse particles of 126.4 ± 7.2 nm (polydispersity index, PDI, 0.14). The zwitterionic corona limited plasma protein adsorption to 12.6 ± 1.5 μg mg-1 (4.6-fold lower than jetPEI/mRNA), kept hemolysis at 0.8 ± 0.2%, and extended the serum half-life of the mRNA to ≈27.4 h, roughly 9-fold longer than naked mRNA. Release was gated by both triggers: 86.5 ± 3.7% of the cargo was released within 8 h under 10 mM GSH, whereas leakage under physiological conditions remained ≤ 12%; in a 4 h matrix, pH 5.5 plus 10 mM GSH released 85 ± 6.8% versus 12 ± 1.5% at pH 7.4 without GSH. In B16F10 cells, the nanocomplex was taken up in a dose- and energy-dependent manner, entered the lysosomal compartment, and escaped over time in a manner consistent with imidazole-mediated proton-sponge buffering (a hypothesis; intralysosomal pH was not measured directly), producing a peak firefly luciferase (FLuc) expression of 56,140 ± 3280 RLU mg-1 protein at 24 h, about 1.5-fold higher than jetPEI/mRNA, with 93.6 ± 3.9% cell viability and 6.7 ± 1.2% lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release. In B16F10-bearing albino C57BL/6 mice, a single intravenous dose produced tumor-dominant bioluminescence (peak 5.7 × 106 photons s-1 at 6 h), a tumor enrichment index of 1.22 ± 0.18 (vs 0.31 ± 0.03 for jetPEI/mRNA) and 2.42 × 107 FLuc mRNA copies μg-1 tumor RNA at 12 h, while all 7-day safety indicators remained at phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) levels. These results demonstrate that a single zwitterionic nanocomplex can integrate stealth, dual-triggered release, and endosomal escape for safe, tumor-enriched mRNA delivery. While this study focuses on delivery performance and reporter gene expression, it lays a solid foundation for future therapeutic applications with functional mRNA.

papers.title: Molecular surveillance of Bartonella species, Coxiella burnetii, and orthohantaviruses in wild small mammals and their associated chigger mites in South Korea.
papers.abstract: Wild small mammals are important hosts of diverse zoonotic pathogens. Molecular surveillance incorporating both small mammals and their associated ectoparasites can provide information on pathogen detection at the wildlife-ectoparasite interface. In this study, 1,444 wild small mammals and 12,869 associated chigger mites, analyzed as 680 host-associated pools, were collected from 17 sites in South Korea between 2022 and 2025. Samples were examined for Bartonella spp., Coxiella burnetii, and orthohantaviruses using PCR- and RT-PCR-based methods, followed by sequence and phylogenetic analyses. The predominant small-mammal species, Apodemus agrarius, accounted for 84.9% of captured small mammals. DNA related to Bartonella schoenbuchensis was detected in 473 of 680 chigger mite pools (69.6%), whereas DNA related to Bartonella bacilliformis, Bartonella henselae, and Bartonella taylorii was detected in three of 1,444 small-mammal liver samples (0.2%) for each taxon. DNA of Coxiella burnetii was detected in 51 of 1,444 liver samples (3.5%), all collected during the autumn 2024 survey. Orthohantavirus RNA was detected in 37 small mammals (2.6%), predominantly in A. agrarius (35/37, 94.6%), with the remaining two detections in Crocidura spp. (2/37, 5.4%), and in three chigger mite pools (0.4%). To our knowledge, these findings provide the first molecular evidence of DNA related to B. schoenbuchensis in host-associated chigger mite pools and document previously unreported DNA related to B. bacilliformis and B. henselae in wild small-mammal liver samples in South Korea. The results provide descriptive baseline data for wildlife-based molecular surveillance; they do not establish seasonal patterns, individual-mite infection prevalence, or vector competence.

papers.title: Inhaled anesthetics and severe neurologic complications in individuals with Venezuelan maternal ancestry carrying the mitochondrial MT-ND4 m.11232 T > C variant: a systematic review.
papers.abstract: Severe neurologic injury after uncomplicated general anesthesia in previously healthy patients is rare. Since 2021, reports from South America and later from North America and Europe have described catastrophic neurologic deterioration and death after routine general anesthesia in children and adults with Venezuelan maternal ancestry. A homoplasmic mitochondrial DNA variant, MT-ND4 m.11232 T > C (p.Leu158Pro), affecting complex I of the electron transport chain, has emerged as the leading candidate susceptibility factor. This systematic review identified, appraised, and synthesized available evidence linking inhaled anesthetics, in particular sevoflurane, with severe perioperative neurologic complications in carriers of this variant and in individuals with Venezuelan maternal ancestry. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261471143), with searches of major biomedical databases, gray literature, and variant databases. The evidence describes a consistent but incompletely characterized syndrome defined by maternal Venezuelan ancestry, apparent preoperative health, predominant sevoflurane exposure, delayed emergence, and severe basal ganglia injury with frequent death. In patient-derived fibroblasts and cybrids, sevoflurane markedly suppressed complex I-dependent respiration, whereas propofol did not. Incidence, penetrance, and agent-specific risk remain uncertain. Cautious perioperative strategies that avoid volatile anesthetics appear justified.

papers.title: Precision Neurology in Alzheimer's Disease: Genomics to Drug Optimization for Effective Therapeutic Intervention.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) exhibits high clinical and biological heterogeneity, which complicates the development of one-size-fits-all therapeutic strategies. Standard trial designs can mask subgroup-specific effects, highlighting the need to move towards precision neurology entailing multisystem genomics, biomarkers, and artificial intelligence (AI) integrative signals. The aim of the study is to critically synthesize and evaluate emerging strategies for drug optimization and individual therapeutic algorithms informed by genomic architecture, pharmacogenomics (PGx), and polygenic risk scores (PRS) with the opinion to resolve the controversy and unanswered question. Amplify the convergence into amyloid processing, lipid metabolism, and innate immunity seen from monogenic mutations and over 80 GWAS risk loci. Genotyping of CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 variants permits pharmacogenomic stratifications for the optimization of cholinesterase inhibitor and psychotropic dosing, thereby reducing adverse events. Variants of the alleles APOE ε4 and immune-related factors (e.g., FCGR3A) are significant in predicting the effects of ARIA associated with amyloid on anti-amyloid immunotherapy outcomes. PRS and deep phenotyping (including digital and fluid-based biomarkers) allow for the identification of unique biological endotypes (e.g., tau-dominant vs. vascular-inflammatory) that improve clinical trial enrichment and prognostication. This framework delineates molecular endotypes and translates CYP2D6 or APOE stratification into drug dosing and ARIA risk predictions. These biomarker-driven strategies shift AD management from a passive, reactive therapeutic scheme to an active, personalized one. Utilization of high-dimensional data streams via AI-driven learning health systems converts AD management from a reactive, symptom-based model to that which is proactive and hallmark biomarker-driven precision.

papers.title: Inherited tubulopathies: molecular mechanisms, pathophysiology, and emerging therapeutic strategies.
papers.abstract: Inherited renal tubulopathies comprise a heterogeneous group of rare monogenic disorders characterized by impaired tubular transport, electrolyte imbalance, and disrupted nephron homeostasis. These disorders involve abnormalities in ion channels, transporters, receptors, intracellular trafficking pathways, and cellular organelles, leading to diverse clinical manifestations including salt wasting, metabolic acidosis, abnormal potassium and calcium handling, nephrocalcinosis, and progressive kidney dysfunction. Despite major advances in next-generation sequencing and functional genomics, the molecular basis of a considerable proportion of inherited tubulopathies remains unresolved. This diagnostic gap reflects the complexity of renal tubular biology, including regulatory genomic variants, incomplete genotype-phenotype correlations, and the involvement of previously unrecognized disease mechanisms. A comprehensive understanding of the genetic and molecular pathways underlying hereditary tubulopathies is essential for improving diagnosis, enabling early intervention, and developing targeted therapies. This review summarizes recent advances in the genetics, pathophysiology, and cellular mechanisms of inherited tubulopathies, with particular emphasis on organelle dysfunction, mitochondrial and lysosomal abnormalities, intracellular trafficking defects, and emerging therapeutic strategies. Furthermore, we discuss the potential of precision medicine, gene-based therapies, and kidney organoid platforms to advance the diagnosis and management of these disorders.

papers.title: First Detection of the Perithecial Stage of Eutypa lata in Chilean Vineyards.
papers.abstract: The sexual stage of Eutypa lata, the causal agent of Eutypa dieback of grapevine, has not been documented previously in Chile, limiting understanding of its epidemiology and disease cycle in this region. The objective of this study was to investigate the occurrence of E. lata perithecia in Chilean vineyards and to confirm the pathogenicity of ascospores. Between 2022 and 2025, surveys were conducted in 36 commercial vineyards in the Maule Region, and perithecia of E. lata were detected on dead grapevine wood in one vineyard. Morphological characterization revealed globose black perithecia containing cylindrical, long-stalked asci and allantoid, hyaline, aseptate ascospores typical of E. lata. Molecular analyses based on ITS and β-tubulin sequences confirmed the identity of isolates obtained from ascospores. Ascospore discharge from perithecia was observed under moist laboratory conditions, and pathogenicity was evaluated under greenhouse and field conditions. In both assays, ascospores induced necrotic lesions in grapevine wood, and the pathogen was successfully reisolated and reidentified, fulfilling Koch's postulates. The detection of perithecia and the completion of Koch's postulates using ascospores provide evidence that E. lata completes its sexual cycle in Chilean vineyards and demonstrate that ascospores produced from naturally occurring perithecia are pathogenic to grapevine. These findings have important implications for disease management, particularly highlighting the need to protect pruning wounds during periods favorable for ascospore release.

papers.title: Immunologically optimized Zmp1 peptides reveal a translational serological biomarker platform for tuberculosis diagnosis across disease manifestations.
papers.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis remains challenging, particularly for extrapulmonary TB (EPTB), where invasive sampling, low bacillary burden, and limited sensitivity of nucleic acid-based tests in peripheral specimens hinder timely detection. Here, we report an immunology-driven strategy for biomarker discovery and development of a peptide-based serological assay targeting Mycobacterium tuberculosis zinc metalloprotease-1 (Zmp1). Based on the principle that antigenic regions containing overlapping B-cell and CD4⁺T-cell epitopes can promote strong antibody responses through linked recognition and cognate T-cell help, we used an immunoinformatics pipeline to identify two nested immunodominant Zmp1 peptide regions, Mtb-Zp-NT and Mtb-Zp-CT, enriched for overlapping B- and T-cell epitopes.Their diagnostic potential was evaluated using ELISA-based serological assays. A blinded pilot study (N = 137) demonstrated clear discrimination between active TB and TB-recovered individuals. An expanded validation cohort (N = 875), identified from screening approximately 6,086 individuals, included pulmonary TB (PTB), EPTB, TB-recovered individuals, household contacts, non-specific infection/inflammation, and healthy controls. Receiver operating characteristic analyses, supported by DeLong and bootstrap comparisons, demonstrated superior diagnostic performance of the peptide assays compared with Mtb-FL-Zmp1. Mtb-Zp-CT showed the highest accuracy (AUC = 0.93), with > 93% specificity and ~ 76% sensitivity.These findings establish immunologically optimized Zmp1 peptides as promising serological biomarkers for TB, including EPTB. Although further optimization may be required to meet WHO target product profiles, their high specificity supports potential use as an adjunctive diagnostic, particularly for EPTB, and as components of future multi-antigen panels. More broadly, this study demonstrates how mechanistically informed epitope selection can facilitate translation of pathogen-specific immune signatures into minimally invasive diagnostic platforms.

papers.title: Pathogen co-infections and disease complexes in cotton: Environmental drivers, diagnostics and research priorities for disease management.
papers.abstract: Cotton production has long faced multiple-pathogen disease scenarios. These include disease complexes where multiple pathogens are involved, accelerating disease progression, altering symptom expression, and reducing the effectiveness of disease management options. These complexes include cotton root rot, vascular wilt, leaf spot, and boll rot. This Feature Article explores plant-pathogen and pathogen-pathogen interactions in cotton disease complexes and the factors that influence them. It also discusses advances in molecular diagnostics, such as pathogen assemblage profiling, which enables more accurate detection and measurement of co-infections, thereby improving risk evaluation and informing targeted disease management practices. Drawing on evidence from cotton-growing regions worldwide, particular attention is given to the relevance and implications of pathogen co-infection and disease complexes for Australian cotton production systems. Recognizing and managing pathogen co-infections and disease complexes, rather than addressing individual pathogens in isolation, provides a framework for more sustainable cotton production systems and enhances the ability to anticipate and respond to evolving crop health challenges under changing conditions driven by climate change, global trade, and agricultural intensification.

papers.title: Pathogen identification and resistance gene expression tests using ASTar remnant bacterial suspension in gram-negative contrived positive blood cultures.
papers.abstract: Rapid pathogen identification, resistance detection, and susceptibility profiling improve antimicrobial prescribing and associated outcomes, but fragmented workflows lead to inefficiencies and are costly. We evaluated a research-use-only (RUO) approach using ASTar remnant bacterial suspension from routine antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) for matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) pathogen identification and lateral flow assay (LFA)-based detection of targeted resistance mechanisms. Gram-negative bacterial strains from reference and curated resistance collections (CDC1, ARLG2, and ATCC3) ( n = 129) were contrived into blood culture bottles and processed in the ASTar System using the ASTar BC G- Kit (Q-linea AB, Sweden). Under RUO conditions, remnant bacterial suspensions were collected ~1-2 h after ASTar run initiation and analyzed using NG Test CTX-M Multi, NG Test CARBA-5, NG Test Acineto-5 RUO, and MALDI-TOF MS. Mean (±SD) remnant suspension volume was 2,722 μL (±300 µL). All samples yielded high-confidence MALDI-TOF MS scores (>2.0), with five initially scoring <2.0 and resolving on repeat testing. LFA results showed full agreement with reference isolates for blaCTX-M positive/negative (32/32) and with 60 or 61 target carbapenemase-positive/negative isolates. Testing of a subset of samples to mimic reflex workflows with ASTar phenotypic results did not affect LFA performance ( n = 35; 23 Enterobacterales, 3 Pseudomonas aeruginosa , and 9 Acinetobacter baumannii ). Cost savings can be realized versus commercial multiplex PCR. This integrated approach of ~6 h rapid phenotypic AST with same-run identification and resistance detection (1-2 h from instrument start) or reflex testing upon availability of ASTar results may support earlier susceptibility results and offer cost savings to current workflows.IMPORTANCERapid, integrated diagnostic workflows are recommended and essential for improving patient outcomes in bloodstream infections, where delays in pathogen identification and resistance detection can compromise timely antimicrobial therapy. Current workflows often rely on multiple platforms, increasing turnaround time and laboratory burden. Additionally, the clinical impact of rapid diagnostic results is dependent on timely interpretation and implementation within antimicrobial stewardship frameworks, which may involve complex decision algorithms. This study demonstrates that remnant bacterial suspensions generated during routine antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) using the ASTar System can be recovered and utilized for rapid matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry and lateral flow assay-based resistance detection. By enabling pathogen identification and/or resistance detection within ~1-2 h of AST initiation or resistance detection via reflex testing, this approach reduces duplicate sample testing and may enable earlier access to rapid microbiological results.

papers.title: Molecular detection of Borrelia puertoricensis and a Coxiella endosymbiont in Ornithodoros puertoricensis from northern Veracruz, Mexico.
papers.abstract: Tick-borne relapsing fever (TBRF) is a neglected zoonosis caused by Borrelia spp. and transmitted by soft ticks of the genus Ornithodoros. Although Mexico has a long history of human TBRF, the current distribution of relapsing fever borreliae and their associated vectors remains poorly understood, particularly in the Mexican Gulf Coast region. This study investigated the presence of tick-borne bacteria in ticks collected at a​ veterinary clinic in northern Veracruz, Mexico. A total of 164 Ornithodoros puertoricensis ticks were identified using morphological characteristics and 16 S mitochondrial ribosomal RNA sequencing. DNA extracts were screened by conventional PCR for Borrelia, Rickettsia, Bartonella, Coxiella, and Ehrlichia/Anaplasma, followed by DNA sequencing and phylogenetic analyses of positive samples. Borrelia puertoricensis DNA was detected in six ticks (3.66%), in four nymphs and two females. Phylogenetic analyses of the flaB gene confirmed that all sequences clustered within the B. puertoricensis clade with strong bootstrap support. In addition, a Coxiella endosymbiont was detected and assigned to clade B based on 16 S rRNA phylogenetic reconstruction, representing the first molecular evidence of this lineage in O. puertoricensis. None of the DNA samples were positive for Rickettsia, Bartonella, Ehrlichia, or Anaplasma. These findings provide the first molecular evidence of B. puertoricensis and a Coxiella clade B endosymbiont in O. puertoricensis from Veracruz, extending the known distribution of both microorganisms in Mexico. The detection of these bacteria in ticks collected at a veterinary clinic capable of treating wild animals highlights the importance of integrated acarological and molecular surveillance at wildlife-domestic animal-human interfaces to improve understanding of the ecology and public health significance of neglected tick-borne zoonoses.

papers.title: Type II GM1 Gangliosidosis with Intrafamilial Variability: A Case Series of Five Affected Siblings.
papers.abstract: GM1 gangliosidosis is a rare, autosomal recessive, progressive, neurosomatic lysosomal storage disorder caused by GLB1 gene variants. The disease demonstrates significant phenotypic heterogeneity, with poor genotype-phenotype correlation. We describe a familial case series of five affected siblings presenting with a variable spectrum of disease manifestations. Clinical evaluation was performed in all siblings, whereas biochemical investigations and neuroimaging were performed in the proband and next-generation testing was performed in two severely affected sibling. Variant interpretation was carried out using standard American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) criteria and phenotype based re-annotation tool. Genetic testing identified compound heterozygous GLB1 variants - c.1325G > A and c.326G > C, confirming the diagnosis of GM1 gangliosidosis. Although the age of onset was similar (6-7 years) in most siblings, variability was observed in disease severity, neurological manifestations and progression. This series highlights the importance of molecular diagnosis in children presenting with unexplained neuroregression. Early genetic confirmation facilitates appropriate genetic counselling, supportive care and prenatal diagnosis.

papers.title: Development and clinical validation of a multiplex PCR-based targeted next-generation sequencing panel for simultaneous DNA/RNA pathogen detection in respiratory tract infections: a comprehensive performance evaluation.
papers.abstract: Lower respiratory tract infections (LRTI) remain a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, with approximately 62 % of cases lacking definitive etiological diagnoses via conventional methods. This study aimed to develop and validate a multiplex PCR-based targeted next-generation sequencing (mp-tNGS) panel for comprehensive pathogen detection in respiratory samples. We conducted a combined retrospective (n=209) and prospective (n=256) study involving 465 bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) samples from patients with suspected LRTI. The mp-tNGS panel was designed to detect 277 clinically relevant pathogens, integrating simultaneous DNA/RNA co-detection and single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-based contamination control. Diagnostic performance was evaluated against conventional microbiological tests (CMTs) and metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS). The mp-tNGS assay revealed a limit of detection (LoD) of 25 copies/mL for bacteria/fungi and 50 copies/mL for viruses, with acceptable precision (intrabatch CV=9.42 %; interbatch CV=26.03 %). A novel SNP-based bioinformatics pipeline achieved exceptional discriminative performance (AUC=0.992) for distinguishing true infections from contamination. Compared with CMTs and mNGS, mp-tNGS showed superior sensitivity (93.59 %, 95 % CI: 90.81-95.73 %), particularly for viruses (AUC=0.92 vs. 0.845). The assay reliably identified fastidious pathogens (e.g., Pneumocystis jirovecii and Legionella pneumophila ) and predicted antimicrobial resistance (97.08 % concordance with phenotypic testing). We developed an mp-tNGS panel with diagnostic performance comparable to that of mNGS. The panel integrates broad pathogen coverage, rapid turnaround time, machine learning-based false-positive reduction, and concordance with phenotypic susceptibility testing, positioning it as a promising molecular diagnostic tool for LRTI.

papers.title: Nationwide molecular survey of Babesia and Theileria DNA in wild rodents and mites collected from rodents in Korea.
papers.abstract: Piroplasm parasites of the genera Babesia and Theileria are widely distributed in wildlife and are maintained through complex host-vector transmission systems. Rodents play important roles as reservoir hosts for various arthropod-borne pathogens; however, comparative investigations integrating multiple host compartments and host-associated ectoparasites remain limited. In this study, we conducted a nationwide molecular survey of Babesia and Theileria species in wild rodents and mites collected from rodents in Korea. Rodent blood and liver tissues, together with mite pools, were examined using PCR-based detection methods, and spatial and seasonal variation in pathogen detection patterns was evaluated. Babesia microti was detected in both rodent blood and liver tissues, with higher positivity in blood and marked spatial and seasonal heterogeneity. The higher positivity observed in blood was consistent with the intraerythrocytic biology of B. microti, although differences in analytical sensitivity between sample types were not evaluated. Theileria capreoli DNA was detected exclusively at low frequency in mite pools, whereas Theileria luwenshuni DNA was detected at low frequency in both rodents and mite pools. Because mites are not established biological vectors of these Theileria species, detections in mite pools were interpreted as molecular occurrence rather than evidence of transmission or vector competence. Significant regional and seasonal variation was observed in blood and mite samples; however, overall detection frequencies were low, warranting cautious ecological interpretation. This nationwide, multi-compartment assessment highlights the ecological complexity of piroplasm circulation in wildlife systems and underscores the importance of integrated surveillance approaches when interpreting parasite DNA detection in arthropod assemblages.

papers.title: Draft genome sequence of basidiomycete yeast Rhodotorula mucilaginosa DH4148 from a patient with fungemia.
papers.abstract: Rhodotorula mucilaginosa is a basidiomycete yeast with ecological and emerging clinical relevance. Here, we report a high-quality de novo genome assembly of R. mucilaginosa strain DH4148 isolated from a patient with fungemia.

papers.title: A Portable, Quick-Visualization Platform for Field Detection of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense Tropical Race 4 ( Foc TR4) in Banana.
papers.abstract: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense ( Foc ) is a soilborne fungal pathogen that causes Fusarium wilt of banana (FWB), leading to multiple outbreaks worldwide and resulting in severe economic losses. In the absence of any effective fungicides or soil disinfectants for this disease, rapid in-field detection of this pathogen is essential for early intervention and containment. However, current in-field detection methods still rely on instruments, making the process time-consuming and complex. Herein, we developed a portable and ultra-fast detection assay for Foc Tropical Race 4 (TR4), the most destructive Foc lineage, based on recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with lateral-flow dipstick (LFD) readout. We identified a TR4-specific DNA fragment as the diagnostic target and prepared crude templates using a room-temperature lysis buffer, eliminating the need for DNA purification. All RPA components, except the template primer-probe mix and magnesium acetate, were lyophilized in a single Eppendorf tube to simplify the workflow and avoid step-by-step reagent addition, allowing the reaction to be conducted in the field by hand or using a portable metal bath. The developed RPA-LFD system offers a high specificity toward Foc TR4, showing no cross-reactivity with other Foc strains, and achieved a limit of detection of 10 fg/μl in the field. This sensitivity enables the detection of infections in asymptomatic plants at early stages. This platform provides a convenient, ultra-fast, and user-friendly tool for on-site Foc TR4 surveillance and supports timely management decisions to curb the spread of FWB.

papers.title: Deep Learning-Enabled Magnetic Bead-Capture Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization Enables Multiplex Identification and Digital Counting of Pathogenic Bacteria.
papers.abstract: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are among the most prevalent infectious diseases worldwide. For complicated and antimicrobial-resistant cases, timely diagnosis is critical for guiding targeted therapy and improving patient outcomes. While conventional urine culture suffers from prolonged turnaround times and low positive detection rates, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) has emerged as a rapid, highly specific alternative. However, its clinical application remains hindered by complicated sample pretreatment, insufficient sensitivity that often requires pre-enrichment by culture, and subjective bias in manual interpretation. To address these bottlenecks, we developed deep learning-enabled magnetic bead-capture fluorescence in situ hybridization (DeepMag-FISH), a culture-free platform that employs artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted digital counting for rapid identification and single-bacterium enumeration of pathogens. We adopted soluble β2-glycoprotein I (sβ2GPI)-coated magnetic beads for efficient pathogen enrichment, and utilized a modular dual-probe labeling strategy for multiplexed hybridization, thus enabling highly specific molecular labeling. Additionally, we integrated this sample processing pipeline with a YOLOv11-based deep learning framework for automatic multiscale feature extraction and precise single-bacterium counting. Validated using spiked urine specimens, DeepMag-FISH clearly differentiated Escherichia coli, Vibrio parahaemolyticus, and Klebsiella pneumoniae with negligible spectral crosstalk. The platform reaches a detection capability of 30 CFU/mL, completing the entire workflow, including all magnetic separation and washing steps, within approximately 3.5 h. By combining magnetic bead-based pathogen enrichment with AI-driven image analysis, this approach mitigates matrix interference and subjective bias in conventional methods, offering a rapid and quantitative approach for pathogen detection in spiked urine samples. Beyond UTI management, DeepMag-FISH may also be explored for potential applications in other fields, such as bloodstream infection diagnosis and food safety monitoring.

papers.title: Genetic and environmental etiology of pediatric and adult-onset multiple sclerosis.
papers.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic demyelinating disease of the central nervous system with complex etiology shaped by both genetic susceptibility and environmental exposures. This review synthesizes classic and emerging literature to provide an integrated framework for understanding MS risk, with emphasis on gene-environment interactions and their contribution to disease. We compile a comprehensive linkage disequilibrium-expanded MS genetic risk variant set identified through genome-wide association studies, including annotation of risk alleles. We discuss insights obtained from functional genomics studies that illuminate genotype-dependent regulatory mechanisms. Environmentally, we assess evidence implicating infectious agents (most notably Epstein-Barr virus) as well as vitamin D insufficiency, obesity, smoking, heavy metal exposure, and the gut microbiome, highlighting epidemiologic associations and areas where mechanistic understanding remains limited. We highlight current knowledge on individuals with pediatric-onset MS (POMS), a population underrepresented in etiologic studies despite its distinct clinical and immunological features. We compare genetic burden, environmental exposures, and immunopathology between pediatric- and adult-onset MS, identifying shared determinants as well as age-specific risk modifiers. Finally, we propose important future directions, including improved ancestry and age-range representation, functional validation of risk loci, and the use of treatment-naïve, tissue-derived patient samples.

papers.title: Proteomic Remodeling and Altered Brain Energy Metabolic Homeostasis in TP53-Knockout Syrian Golden Hamsters.
papers.abstract: The tumor suppressor TP53 is a critical regulator of cell-cycle control, apoptosis, senescence, and cellular metabolism. However, its role in maintaining energy homeostasis in normal tissues, particularly in the brain, remains incompletely understood. In this study, proteomic profiling of brain, leukocytes, pancreas, and plasma from p53 knock-out (p53-/- ) Syrian Golden Hamsters (Mesocrecetus auratus) was investigated and compared with wild-type (WT) hamsters. We found a larger alternation in differentially expressed proteins in brain samples, while the pancreas showed a higher proportion of upregulated proteins. Functional enrichment analyses revealed significant changes in metabolic pathways, including oxidative phosphorylation and NAD(P)-binding processes. Notably, energy metabolism-associated pathways were predominantly downregulated in the brain of TP53-/- hamsters, involving candidate proteins Bcl2l1, Mta1, Nqo1, and Ube3a. Validation experiments confirmed dysregulated expression of these proteins at both transcript and protein levels, which is highly related to mitochondrial functions. ATP measurements further demonstrated unbalanced energy homeostasis in TP53-deficient brain tissue. The proteomic atlas of the p53-/- new animal model in this work provides a novel genetic and functional foundation for understanding the role of TP53 in mental disorders, which can be potentially significant for biological science and medicine.

papers.title: Helminth infections: from genomic discovery to public health interventions.
papers.abstract: Helminths infect more than a billion people worldwide and cause substantial chronic morbidity, impaired physical and cognitive development in children, and reduced wellbeing and economic productivity, particularly in low-income and middle-income countries. Preventive chemotherapy, sanitation, vector control, and integrated programmes have substantially reduced infection intensity and morbidity in many settings, although sustaining these gains and advancing towards elimination require complementary tools. Advances in genomics, multiomics, and computational biology have added a complementary, data-rich dimension to established parasitology, supporting systematic target identification, improved molecular diagnostics, and new insights into transmission and drug response. In this Review, we examine how these approaches are reshaping the study of helminth infections and the implications of these approaches for diagnosis, treatment, and control. Translating these technological and scientific advances into effective interventions still requires representative data, experimental and field validation, accessible infrastructure, trained personnel, and sustainable implementation, particularly in resource-constrained settings. Ultimately, integrating genomic and molecular discoveries with clinical, epidemiological, and public health strategies within a One Health framework will be central to achieving measurable and sustained improvements in helminth control.

papers.title: Q&A with Dr. Philip Awadalla.
papers.abstract: Editor-in-Chief Laura Zahn asked Dr. Philip Awadalla from the University of Oxford to tell us about his research and his recent Cell Genomics paper, "Pre-diagnosis plasma cell-free DNA reveals early signatures of prostate and breast cancer risk up to eight years prior to clinical detection."

papers.title: Comparative genomic analysis of Acinetobacter baumannii strains suggests possible human risk with environmentally distributed sequence type 1.
papers.abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii belongs to clinically significant opportunistic pathogens that has already been emerged as a major global health threat due to its remarkable capacity to acquire and disseminate antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Understanding the phenotypic and genotypic relationships between its clinical and environmental strains, hence is essential for tracking the dissemination of resistant strains and also for mitigating the spread of AMR. Comprehensive surveillance of clinical and environmental samples for A. baumannii is essential to identify the evolution of clinically relevant strains. In the study, detailed morphological characterization, antimicrobial susceptibility testing and biofilm formation assays were performed to screen the pathogenic strains of A. baumannii from clinical and environmental samples. Phenotypic screening conducted in the study has yielded 85 strains of A. baumannii, which included isolates from clinical (60), soil (16), and water (9) samples. Among these, 23 strains were multi-drug resistant (MDR), with 21 having clinical, and 2 with environmental origin respectively. Further to this extensively drug resistant (XDR) strain from each clinical and environmental origin was subjected to Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) analysis. Bioinformatic pipelines, including PubMLST, RAST, CARD, MGE, PHASTER, PathogenFinder, and Mauve​ were further used to predict the resistomes, mobile genetic elements, and the functional metabolite biosynthetic potential of sequenced genome. The CARD analysis has further identified clinically significant antibiotic-resistance genes (ARGs) such as bla OXA-23 , bla OXA-69 and lpsB genes, along with plasmids Tn6018, ISAba26 and ISAba13 that carries genes related to major antibiotic resistance and gene encoding AbaQ efflux pump in the sequenced genome. Alignment between WGS data of sequenced A. baumannii strains such as C3 and E2 has further been carried out along with the comparative phylogenomic dataset composed of global (29) and Indian (16) A. baumannii genomes retrieved from from BV-BRC. Global phylogenetic analysis has demonstrated the environmental strain E2 to come under a novel Sequence Type ST3394 Pas . This was having close alignment with a distinct clinical clade containing the high-risk international clones GC1/ ST1. The two sequenced strains have also been observed to have shared K- and O- loci as similar to other clinically relevant ST1 clade. Subsequent pangenome and Mauve analyses have further confirmed the genetic homology and minimal structural rearrangements between the selected environmental and clinical strains of A. baumannii. The observed similarities suggest a possible epidemiological relationship or shared lineage between clinical and environmental A. baumannii strains isolated in the study, which need to be further confirmed by large scale isolation, comparison and analysis.

papers.title: Evaluating facility-level variability in urinary antimicrobial susceptibility patterns in long-term care homes in Ontario, Canada.
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance surveillance in long-term care homes is limited by its reliance on organism-specific summaries, most commonly Escherichia coli , which may not reflect the broader microbiological landscape in these settings. We evaluated how E. coli -based urinary susceptibility compared with weighted-incidence syndromic combination antibiograms (WISCA), a composite measure incorporating multiple pathogens, across 627 Ontario long-term care homes in 2023. Facility-level antimicrobial susceptibilities to eight antibiotics were estimated using 23,750 urinary isolates, with missing data addressed through imputation, and estimates stabilized using random-intercept logistic regression models. E. coli accounted for a mean of 50.6% (standard deviation = 1.9) of urinary isolates, with the remaining 49.5% mainly comprising Klebsiella pneumoniae (16.6% [0.8]), Proteus mirabilis (11.9% [1.2]), Enterococcus faecalis (6.6% [2.1]), and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (6.1% [0.1]). Organism-specific susceptibility varied substantially across antibiotics, particularly for ciprofloxacin susceptibility in P. mirabilis (78.7% [13.1]) and E. faecalis (48.9% [11.5]), and nitrofurantoin susceptibility in K. pneumoniae (48.5% [9.0]). Compared with E. coli -based estimates, WISCA susceptibilities were lower for seven of eight antibiotics, most notably for nitrofurantoin (WISCA: 70.6% vs E. coli: 96.8%). These findings suggest that reliance on E. coli alone may not fully capture facility-level urinary susceptibility patterns, as variation in pathogen distribution and organism-specific antibiotic susceptibilities across homes can produce substantially different susceptibility estimates. WISCA provides a more representative and stable measure by incorporating pathogen diversity and weighting organism prevalence. Integrating this into antimicrobial resistance surveillance for long-term care homes may improve the detection of emerging resistance trends and better inform antimicrobial stewardship strategies by identifying variable organism-antibiotic combinations.IMPORTANCEAntimicrobial resistance is a growing concern in long-term care homes, where infections are common, and antibiotics are frequently used. Surveillance in these settings often relies on Escherichia coli to estimate how well antibiotics will work, but this approach may not capture the range of urinary pathogens encountered in these settings, differences in resistance between organisms, or how these differences can vary across long-term care homes. In this study, E. coli represented only about half of the urinary infections, while other organisms including Klebsiella pneumoniae and Proteus mirabilis demonstrated differing susceptibility levels across antibiotics. These findings support the value of organism-inclusive surveillance, such as weighted-incidence syndromic combination antibiograms, to provide a more comprehensive picture of resistance and better inform antimicrobial stewardship strategies in long-term care homes.

papers.title: Multimodal single-cell analyses reveal distinct fusion-regulated transcriptional programs in Ewing sarcoma.
papers.abstract: Ewing sarcoma (EwS) is a fusion-driven malignancy, peaking in adolescence. Although EwS tumors are driven uniquely by EWS::FLI1 and related fusions, patient outcomes vary greatly. If and how tumor plasticity of EWS::FLI1-regulated transcriptional signatures contributes to disease progression is not known. To address this, we utilized a single-cell co-assay of RNA and chromatin accessibility (ATAC) sequencing to identify gene regulatory networks in EwS. By comprehensively characterizing regulatory elements across cell lines, we identified multiple unique modules of gene regulation. Differential usage and prevalence of these modules was evident across cell lines, associated with distinct epigenetic and transcriptomic signatures, and in specific cases, modifiable by exogenous TGF-β. When we examined primary EwS patient tumors, we observed these same regulatory modules were variably enriched both across and within tumors, highlighting the existence of intratumoral heterogeneity in gene regulatory networks. Our findings demonstrate that multiple, co-existing transcriptional programs shape the phenotypic diversity of EwS and suggest that the balance between these networks may have important implications for clinical outcomes and targeted therapy development.

papers.title: In-field crop disease surveillance: from phenotypes to molecules.
papers.abstract: Climate change and increasing ecological complexity intensify crop diseases, causing severe yield losses and threatening global food security. Timely and accurate in-field surveillance is essential for early warning and effective management of crop diseases. Advances in sensing technologies, flexible electronics, and synthetic biology are transforming crop disease surveillance from phenotypes to molecules. In this review, we first summarize major crop pathogens and pests as well as their associated disease biomarkers. We then examine field-deployable molecular detection approaches, including point-of-need assays, drone-equipped platforms, wearable devices, and sentinel plants, which enable in-field, real-time, broad-scale, and long-term surveillance of crop infection. We assess their technological readiness and applications in early crop infection detection, field pathogen survey, pesticide application instruction, and investigations of crop stress responses. Finally, we discuss the prospects of miniaturized, high-throughput analytical devices and the Internet of Things, as well as the challenges of translating in-field surveillance technologies into agricultural applications that will reshape crop disease management.

papers.title: A phage-displayed nanobody-based colorimetric-fluorescent dual-readout immunoassay using Eu-micelles for detecting Bacillus cereus in food.
papers.abstract: Bacillus cereus (B. cereus) is a common foodborne pathogen that contaminates agricultural products and induces emetic or diarrheal food poisoning. We report an europium(Eu)-micelle-mediated colorimetric-fluorescent dual-readout nanobody-based immunoassay for B. cereus detection. Four novel B. cereus-specific nanobodies were isolated for the first time from an immune Bactrian camel phage-displayed nanobody library. A sandwich immunoassay was established using a purified soluble nanobody (Nb23) for target capture and a phage-displayed Nb (phage-Nb23) for detection, leveraging an HRP-conjugated anti-M13 antibody to achieve phage-mediated primary signal amplification. Self-assembled Eu-micelles were introduced post-reaction as an independent fluorescent module. HRP-catalyzed oxidation of TMB generated a 652 nm colorimetric signal while concurrently quenching Eu-micelle red emission at 616 nm through a combination of inner filter effects and interfacial excited-state deactivation. Under optimized conditions, the limits of detection were 3.84 × 10 4 CFU/mL for the colorimetric channel and 8.57 × 10 3 CFU/mL for the fluorescent channel, demonstrating a 4.5-fold sensitivity enhancement. Spiked recoveries across diverse food matrices (rice, pork, bean sprouts, and juice) ranged from 92.48% to 116.42%, with relative standard deviations ≤ 5.54%. This dual-readout strategy offers mutual validation and broad applicability for food safety monitoring.

papers.title: Phage Cocktail-Mediated Ultrasensitive Real-Time Electrochemical Whole-Cell Detection of Klebsiella pneumoniae on a SPCE.
papers.abstract: Rapid and selective detection of pathogenic bacteria is essential for timely clinical diagnosis and environmental surveillance. In this work, we report a bacteriophage-assisted electrochemical sensing platform for the selective detection of Klebsiella pneumoniae using an Er2O3/Co3O4/Au/polyethylenimine (PEI)-modified screen-printed carbon electrode (SPCE). The hierarchical nanocomposite was engineered to provide high surface area, enhanced charge transfer kinetics, and abundant functional sites for efficient phage immobilization. PEI served as a cationic linker to facilitate electrostatic attachment of lytic bacteriophages while maintaining their biological activity and host specificity. Upon target recognition, phage-bacteria binding at the electrode interface produced pronounced impedance changes due to interfacial blocking and altered electron transfer dynamics. The developed biosensor exhibited high selectivity for Klebsiella pneumoniae over nontarget bacteria and could distinguish live from dead bacteria. The sensor showed a wide linear detection range of 10-107 CFU/mL with a low detection limit of 7.36 CFU/mL and good repeatability with an RSD of ∼1.17%. The real-world applicability of the sensor was tested using aquarium water samples and demonstrated good performance, with recovery percentages ranging from ∼91.71 to 96.26%. This work establishes a robust nano-bio hybrid interface strategy that integrates rare-earth/transition metal oxide electrocatalysts with phage biorecognition on disposable SPCE platforms. The developed system shows strong potential for point-of-care pathogen monitoring in clinical, environmental, and food safety applications.

papers.title: Multicenter evaluation of the multiplex polymerase chain reaction QIAstat-Dx Meningitis/Encephalitis Panel for the detection of central nervous system pathogens directly in the cerebrospinal fluid.
papers.abstract: Rapid and accurate detection of pathogens causing meningitis/encephalitis (MEN/EN) is critical to improving clinical outcomes. Multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) enables simultaneous detection of multiple pathogens from the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), offering advantages over traditional methods. This multicenter study evaluated the performance of the QIAstat-Dx Meningitis/Encephalitis (ME) Panel versus conventional methods, including the BioFire FilmArray ME (BFME) Panel. The CSF samples from patients with suspected MEN/EN along with contrived samples were tested across 13 sites in Europe/USA. Positive percent agreement (PPA) and negative percent agreement (NPA) between the QIAstat-Dx ME Panel and comparator methods were determined. A total of 1,667 clinical samples (1,527 prospective, 140 archived) were tested. Pathogens were detected by the QIAstat-Dx ME Panel in 115 (7.5%) prospective samples, including Streptococcus pneumoniae (1.1%), Haemophilus influenzae (0.5%), Listeria monocytogenes (0.3%), S. agalactiae (0.2%), Escherichia coli K1 (0.1%), Neisseria meningitidis (0.1%), S. pyogenes (0.1%), enterovirus (1.5%), human herpesvirus-6 (1.0%), herpes simplex virus-2 (0.9%) and -1 (0.3%), varicella zoster virus (0.7%), cytomegalovirus (0.3%), human parechovirus (0.3%), and Cryptococcus gattii/neoformans (0.4%). Overall PPA versus BFME ( n = 1,664) was 85.4%, increasing to 95.3% after discordance resolution. PPA was 100% for N. meningitidis , S. pneumoniae , and S. agalactiae . Overall NPA was 99.9%. Among 1,154 contrived positive samples, only 27 (2.3%) incorrect results were observed. The QIAstat-Dx ME Panel demonstrated high concordance with BFME, supporting its use as a reliable, fully automated multiplex PCR platform for rapid diagnosis of community-acquired MEN/EN.IMPORTANCEThis multicenter study demonstrated that the QIAstat-Dx ME Panel delivers clinical performance comparable to that of the BioFire FilmArray ME (BFME) Panel, supporting its validity as a reliable syndromic molecular diagnostic tool for MEN/EN. With its broad pathogen coverage, rapid turnaround time (TAT), and the ability to provide amplification curves and Ct values, the QIAstat-Dx ME Panel offers a valuable option for broad and timely detection of bacterial, viral, and fungal CNS pathogens. When used alongside the SoC diagnostic methods, this panel has the potential to improve early diagnosis, guide targeted therapy, and support effective clinical management of patients with suspected MEN/EN.

papers.title: Native pathogen-phage networks reveal multilayered defense and gut-active anti-phage immunity.
papers.abstract: Bacteriophages drive pathogen evolution, yet the mechanisms governing phage susceptibility in native bacterial backgrounds, and their consequences within mammalian hosts, remain poorly understood. Here, we mapped >1,000 interactions between 20 diverse Salmonella isolates and 52 wild phages from global disease reservoirs, integrating genome-scale fitness profiling with comparative genomics. Receptor identity and surface phase variation, including Hin-mediated flagellar switching, explained ∼67% of phage susceptibility patterns, identifying cell-surface architecture as the major determinant of phage host range in Salmonella. Among resistance phenotypes not explained by surface features, we discovered anti-phage-packaging agent (AppA), a prophage-encoded defense factor that abrogates phage replication within its native host. AppA inhibits phage DNA packaging through functional mimicry of a terminase assembly interface, revealing a previously unrecognized mechanism of phage defense. AppA is expressed under conditions encountered during mammalian infection and suppresses phage expansion in the murine gut, demonstrating that prophage-encoded single-gene defenses can shape disease outcomes in vivo.

papers.title: Diagnostic challenges in Mycobacterium abscessus pulmonary disease, particularly in patients with cystic fibrosis: toward an integrated precision framework.
papers.abstract: Mycobacterium abscessus has emerged as one of the most formidable pathogens affecting people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF), driven by intrinsic antimicrobial resistance, complex taxonomy, and substantial diagnostic uncertainty. Despite major technological advances, establishing a diagnosis of pulmonary disease remains challenging, as traditional culture-based workflows are constrained by limited sensitivity, prolonged turnaround times. However, recent progress in proteomic and genomic technologies has markedly improved organism detection and taxonomic resolution. This review examines the contemporary diagnostic architecture for M. abscessus pulmonary infection in pwCF, identifying persistent gaps, and proposes a precision-oriented framework in which culture, proteomics, genomics, and host-response biomarkers converge to support earlier and more individualized clinical decision-making.

papers.title: Hyperporphyrin Effect-Driven Bandgap Narrowing in Cationic Fe3O4@ICOF for Boosted Photothermal Immunoassay.
papers.abstract: Molecular orbital engineering tackles the wide bandgaps and limited near-infrared (NIR) response that constrain conventional immunochromatographic assays (ICAs) by precisely tailoring the electronic properties of covalent organic frameworks (COFs), enabling ultrasensitive pathogen detection. Here, we report a methylation-mediated cationization strategy to construct core-shell Fe3O4@ICOF, where a cationic porphyrin COF shell is grown on a magnetic Fe3O4 core. The methylation triggers a hyperporphyrin effect that dramatically narrows the HOMO-LUMO gap from 2.634 eV to 1.997 eV, redirecting energy dissipation toward non-radiative thermal relaxation and yielding an ultrahigh photothermal conversion efficiency of 71.9% under 808 nm irradiation. The magnetic core enables facile enrichment, while the cationic surface promotes electrostatic capture of negatively charged Salmonella, synergistically enhancing sensitivity. Integrating colorimetric and photothermal readouts, the dual-modal ICA achieves detection limits of 100 CFU/mL (colorimetric) and 50 CFU/mL (photothermal), representing 500- to 1000-fold improvement over conventional AuNPs-based ICA, which shows satisfactory recoveries in real food matrices. This work establishes a clear structure-electronics-photothermal performance correlation, providing a design method for high-performance point-of-care pathogen sensors.

papers.title: PAM-Free Programmable Enzymatic Cascade Design Enabling Highly Sensitive CRISPR/Cas12a Lateral Flow Assay for Foodborne Pathogen Detection.
papers.abstract: CRISPR/Cas12a-assisted nucleic acid assays have shown great potential for rapid pathogen detection. However, their implementation in lateral flow assays remains constrained by strict protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) requirements and low-contrast, signal-off readouts. To effectively address these limitations, we present a new PAM-free programmable enzymatic cascade-enabled CRISPR/Cas12a lateral flow assay (PAEC-LFA) for highly sensitive foodborne pathogen detection. In this strategy, target amplification products are enzymatically digested to generate programmable single-stranded DNA activators, enabling PAM-independent Cas12a activation and flexible target recognition. Upon activation, Cas12a exhibits efficient trans-cleavage activity, which subsequently triggers terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT)-mediated extension, forming an enzymatic cascade that amplifies signal output and generates a high-contrast signal-on readout on lateral flow assays. Integrating RPA and enzymatic digestion with PAM-free Cas12a-TdT signal amplification into two sequential one-pot modules simplifies the workflow, minimizes contamination risk, and maintains effective amplification performance. Under optimized conditions, PAEC-LFA achieved detection limits of 1.05 CFU/mL for Salmonella and Staphylococcus aureus, and 3.13 CFU/mL for Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Visual detection limits in spiked food samples reached 10 CFU/mL for all three pathogens. This work establishes a generalizable PAM-free enzymatic cascade framework for highly sensitive CRISPR/Cas12a lateral flow assays, advancing practical pathogen detection in food safety applications.

papers.title: Tick-borne pathogens in Swedish wild boar and their attached ticks: the first detection of Borrelia species in wild boar in northern Europe.
papers.abstract: The wild boar (Sus scrofa) population has expanded in northern Europe, yet their role in the ecology of tick-borne pathogens remains poorly understood. This study investigated the occurrence of Anaplasma phagocytophilum and Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato in 88 Swedish wild boar and their attached Ixodes ricinus ticks by analysing multiple tissues (spleen, heart, urinary bladder and skin) using quantitative PCR. Anaplasma phagocytophilum was detected in 20 (22.7%) wild boar, with infections (i.e. quantitative PCR positive) more common in juveniles than adults. Infection probability was lowest in spring but markedly higher in summer and autumn. Borrelia species DNA was detected in three juvenile males (3.4%), representing the first report of Borrelia species in wild boar in northern Europe. Thirty attached ticks were collected from 17 wild boar. Six ticks carried A. phagocytophilum, five carried Borrelia species, and one was coinfected. Ticks were more likely to be infected when collected from infected wild boar than from uninfected hosts, while feeding duration showed no detectable association with infection in either hosts or ticks. These findings provide new insight into the occurrence of tick-borne pathogens in wild boar and highlight the value of multi-tissue sampling and paired host-tick data for understanding pathogen dynamics in wildlife populations.

papers.title: Applying geographic information systems data linkages for an exposome-wide association study in the Personalized Environment and Genes Study.
papers.abstract: Affordable genomics assays have enabled new study designs such as genome-wide association studies (GWAS), advancing scientific understanding of disease etiology, prevention, and treatment. A standardized process for linking study participants' residential histories with publicly available geospatial environmental data across existing and future epidemiologic cohorts could enable cost-effective geographic information systems (GIS)-based exposome-wide association studies (GIS-ExWAS), similarly expanding scientific understanding of disease. To explore this approach, we used open-source GIS software to link data from 7531 Personalized Environment and Genes Study (PEGS) participants on 11 common disease phenotypes with multiple types of GIS data from various sources to develop 88 GIS-based exposure indicators. We then estimated cross-sectional associations between these exposure indicators and the selected phenotypes using covariate-adjusted logistic regression, inverse probability of treatment weighted (IPTW), and the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) models. The IPTW and LASSO models identified GIS-phenotype associations complementary to those found in a prior ExWAS in questionnaire-based data from the PEGS cohort, including associations between air pollution and cardiovascular disease, as well as novel suggestive associations between several phenotypes and environmental factors not previously assessed by PEGS. Our results suggest GIS linkages can enhance exposome assessment but also highlight key methodological complexities that must be overcome to develop standardized GIS-based ExWAS that can be broadly applied. Developing standardized open-source tools for GIS data linkage and exposure assessment could enhance public health practice, precision medicine, and scientific understanding of the exposome's impacts on health. GIS linkages can enhance exposome assessment and offer benefits for public health and clinical research. Adding GIS-based exposome assessments to survey-based data from cohort studies can help detect exposure-phenotype associations not detectable in survey data alone. Developing a standardized exposome assay based on GIS data would enable low-cost baseline geospatial assessments of environmental quality using only a residential address. Open-source GIS data linkage tools leveraging geospatially linked publicly available data would improve research, clinical practice, and public health.

papers.title: Engineering DNA Nanoflowers with Programmable Architectures: From Design Paradigms to Biosensing.
papers.abstract: It is of great significance to design and fabricate multifunctional engineered nanostructures by loading functional components on demand in a simplified manner, to achieve sensitive and reliable sensing of targets in complex environments. DNA nanoflowers (DNFs) with precisely compartmentalizable design are a type of emerging three-dimensional hybrid nanomaterial. Compared with traditional DNA self-assembly structures, DNF integrates efficient one-step synthesis, significantly enhanced structural robustness, superior biological delivery efficiency, and powerful modular functional integration capabilities. It can break through the limitations of traditional detection methods in terms of insufficient sensitivity and single functionality, and is a promising practical sensing material. This review first provides a concise summary of the synthetic methods and structural advantages of DNFs. On this foundation, a systematic framework is established to elaborate the diverse design paradigms of engineered DNFs, including acyclic, single-ring, and dual- or multiring designs. Furthermore, recent advances in the application of engineered DNFs to in vitro biosensing and bioimaging (especially pathogen imaging) are comprehensively summarized. Finally, perspectives on the current challenges and future development directions of DNF-based biotechnology are articulated, aiming to furnish valuable insights for researchers in relevant disciplines.

papers.title: Risk factors and aetiological agents of community-acquired pneumonia in children under five years in South Asia: A systematic review.
papers.abstract: Pneumonia remains a leading cause of mortality among children under five years in South Asia, a region that, with sub-Saharan Africa, accounts for over half of the world's childhood pneumonia cases. To our knowledge, no prior review has jointly synthesised the risk factors and aetiological agents of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in under-fives specific to this region. This systematic review aimed to identify, critically appraise, and synthesise available evidence on the risk factors and aetiological agents associated with CAP in children under five years of age in South Asian countries. Following PRISMA guidelines, four electronic databases (MEDLINE, PubMed, Global Health, and Web of Science) were systematically searched for studies published between January 2000 and July 2024, with the search updated to January 2026. Quality assessment was performed using the Crowe Critical Appraisal Tool (CCAT), with only high-quality studies (≥75% score) included in the final synthesis. Data were synthesised narratively due to heterogeneity in study designs and outcome measures. From 1196 records identified and 747 studies screened, 16 met the inclusion criteria after quality assessment (8 on risk factors, 8 on aetiology), conducted across five South Asian countries (India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan, Bhutan). Young age (children 0-23 months), malnutrition (particularly underweight and wasting), and incomplete immunisation emerged as the most consistently identified risk factors across studies. Environmental exposures, including indoor air pollution, poor ventilation, and overcrowding, were significant contributors. Viral pathogens predominated in aetiological studies, with respiratory syncytial virus being the most frequently identified pathogen (mean detection rate 29.2%). Blood culture positivity for bacterial pathogens was generally lower (1.5-31.3%; below 13% in four of five studies), with Streptococcus pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus most common among positive cultures. This systematic review demonstrates that childhood CAP in South Asia results from a complex interplay of modifiable host, environmental, and socioeconomic risk factors. Integrated interventions addressing nutrition, immunization coverage, household air pollution, and socioeconomic determinants are essential for reducing the substantial pneumonia burden among South Asian children.

papers.title: Evaluation of antibiotic resistance profiles, biofilm formation capacity and molecular detection of resistance genes in clinical P. aeruginosa isolates recovered from hospitalized patients in Ilam, Iran.
papers.abstract: P. aeruginosa is a leading cause of healthcare-associated infections and is recognized by the WHO as a critical priority pathogen due to its intrinsic and acquired resistance mechanisms and its remarkable capacity for biofilm formation. This study aimed to evaluate antibiotic resistance profiles, biofilm formation capacity, and the molecular detection of resistance genes in clinical P. aeruginosa isolates recovered from hospitalized patients in Ilam, Iran. A total of 44 non-duplicate P. aeruginosa isolates were collected from urine, blood, and sputum specimens between November 2023 and August 2024. Identification used standard microbiological and biochemical tests. Antimicrobial susceptibility was determined by Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion following CLSI guidelines, and colistin MIC was determined by broth microdilution. Biofilm formation was assessed using a microtiter plate assay with crystal violet staining. Major resistance genes, including β-lactamases ( bla -GES, bla -CTX, bla -SHV, bla -TEM), metallo-β-lactamases ( bla -NDM, bla -VIM, bla -IMP), and fluoroquinolone resistance determinants (parC, parE), were detected via PCR. The isolates exhibited high resistance rates to aztreonam (100%), gentamicin (68.2%), and imipenem (59.1%), while amikacin remained the most effective agent (95.5% susceptible). Following broth microdilution, colistin resistance was only 2.3%. Molecular analysis revealed that bla -GES (100%) and parC (95.5%) were the most prevalent resistance genes. followed by bla -CTX (55.5%), bla -SHV (45.5%), bla -TEM (45.5%), parE (36.4%), bla -NDM (13.6%), bla -VIM (13.6%), and bla -IMP (4.5%). Biofilm formation was observed in all isolates: 68.2% weak, 31.8% moderate; no strong producers were identified. A significant association was found between anatomical specimen source and biofilm strength (p = 0.011), with sputum isolates showing the highest moderate biofilm formation (75%). However, no significant association was observed between biofilm phenotype and antibiotic resistance. The coexistence of MDR-associated genes and biofilm-forming ability underscores P. aeruginosa as a critical MDR pathogen. The high prevalence of bla- GES and parC, combined with the association between respiratory origin and moderate biofilm formation, highlights its adaptive success. Continuous surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship, routine colistin MIC testing, and anti-biofilm therapeutic approaches are essential to mitigate the clinical impact of MDR P. aeruginosa infections.

papers.title: First report of Stemphylium eturmiunum causing leaf spot on Eucalyptus tricarpa in Australian native vegetation.
papers.abstract: Eucalyptus spp. dominate Australia's most environmentally and economically significant ecosystems due to their ecological resilience (through post-fire epicormic regeneration), and widespread occurrence in remnant vegetation adjacent to agricultural crops, where they can influence disease dynamics and biosecurity risk (Keane et al. 2000). In March 2025, leaves from epicormic growth of two mature Eucalyptus tricarpa trees exhibiting concolorous 35 mm 2 (15% leaf area) asymmetrical brown, sunken necrotic lesions with dark margins were collected from native vegetation near Anglesea, Victoria (38°22'27" S, 144°14'43" E). Approximately 10% of epicormic leaves of adjacent E. tricarpa within a 100 m radius of the site displayed similar lesions. The leaves were surface sterilized (80% ethanol) and sections from lesion margins were cultured (25°C, one week). Hyphal tips were subcultured onto Potato Dextrose Agar (PDA). One lesion yielded three morphologically distinct isolates, including Alternaria sp., Allelochaeta sp., and Stemphylium sp., the second lesion yielded a further two distinct isolates, including Readeriella sp., and Neofusiccocum eucalypticola . All species isolated are known Eucalyptus pathogens (Crous et al. 2018; Keane et al. 2000), except Stemphylium sp. (UOM26001), which was examined further. This genus comprises important agricultural pathogens but are unknown from Australian native vegetation (Vaghefi et al. 2020). Two week-old PDA cultures had pale salmon mycelium and brown sporulation rings. Microscopic examination revealed hyaline few-septate hyphae, and mid-brown vertically and transversely 2-4-septate globose conidia 23.6 ± 3.38 x 17.6 ± 2.59 µm (21.0 - 30.9 x 12.3 - 22.8 µm), n=16, consistent with Stemphylium spp. (Simmons 2001). DNA was extracted via a modified Qiagen Plant MiniKit protocol (Vaghefi et al. 2024), and PCR and Sanger sequencing was performed for the internal transcribed spacer region and intervening 5.8S (ITS), calmodulin and gapdh with primers ITS1/ITS4 (White et al. 1990), caldf1/caldr2 (Carbone and Kohn 1999), and Gpd1/Gpd2 (Berbee et al. 1999). Sequences were deposited in GenBank as PZ054204 (ITS), PZ055902 (cal), PZ055903 (gapdh). BLAST showed all sequences were identical to Stemphylium eturmiunum reference sequences, including ex-holotype (CBS 109845). Multi-locus phylogenetic analysis was performed using RaxML v8.2.11 and MrBayes v3.2.6 (GTR model and 10 000 bootstrap replicates). UOM26001 clustered with S. eturmiunum isolates, with bootstrap and posterior probability values of 96 and 1.00, respectively. To assess pathogenicity, detached leaf assays were conducted due to constraints in sourcing whole trees for representative in planta assays, and biosecurity restrictions for trials external to a laboratory space. Therefore, following a standard method for Eucalyptus spp. bioassays (Alcova et al. 2026) sprigs of E. tricarpa epicormic growth each had 2 leaves surface sterilized (1% NaClO) and inoculated with 1 mm2 plugs of one week old UOM26001 via wounding (abrasions with sterile scalpel) (n = 6) and non-wounding (n = 6) methods. Negative controls (n = 6) were sterilized, wounded, and inoculated with clean PDA. Sprigs were placed in water and incubated for two weeks (12 - 20°C, 90% humidity, 12hr photoperiod), pathogenicity assays were repeated 3 times, for a total of 6 replicates of each inoculation method, including the control. After 14 days, 3/6 wounded, and 2/6 non-wounded inoculated leaves displayed pale brown necrotic lesions, similar but not identical to the original lesion due to the field symptoms being caused by a disease complex rather than UOM26001 alone. Negative controls were symptom free. Sections from lesion margins were plated onto PDA and incubated for one week at 25°C. Colonies re-isolated from all inoculated symptomatic leaf lesions were identified as S. eturmiunum based on culture and conidia morphology, confirming pathogenicity. Stemphylium eturmiunum is known in Australia and globally as a pathogen of agricultural crops (Vaghefi et al. 2020), but this is the first report on native Eastern Australian vegetation, and on E. tricarpa globally. This suggests S. eturmiunum may threaten post-fire regeneration of native trees by destroying new photosynthetic surfaces. And while this report cannot fully confirm significance for E. tricarpa due to only a single isolate being recovered, the detection in native vegetation expands the host range of S. eturmiunum , indicating E. tricarpa remnant vegetation could act as a pathogen reservoir, facilitating crop infection in Australian agricultural settings.

papers.title: Comparative genomics of the skin microbiome and associated isolates of patients undergoing mastectomy with immediate breast reconstruction.
papers.abstract: Mastectomy with immediate breast implant reconstruction (IBIR) is an increasingly common component of breast cancer treatment; however, these procedures carry a substantial risk of surgical site infections (SSIs) and noninfectious wound complications (NIWCs). We hypothesized that the local skin microbiota may contribute to the development of post-operative complications, in part by serving as a reservoir for pathobionts, such as Staphylococcus epidermidis and Cutibacterium acnes . We collected skin and intraoperative samples from 60 patients undergoing mastectomy with IBIR. To evaluate longitudinal shifts in community composition, we performed 16S rRNA gene sequencing of 151 breast and axilla skin swabs collected at pre- and post-operative time points. Using a comprehensive culture approach, we recovered diverse cultivable organisms and selected 232 S. epidermidis and 130 C. acne s isolates from skin swabs, implant swabs, and seroma fluid for whole-genome sequencing and comparative genomic analysis. We observed perturbations to community structure in the breast and axilla following mastectomy. These shifts were characterized by a significant and persistent depletion of Corynebacterium spp . , which did not resolve in patients who subsequently developed an SSI. We also uncovered outcome-specific genomic signatures in S. epidermidis isolates, which may offer mechanistic insight into the role of this species in SSI and NIWC development. Importantly, we also identified genomic signatures detectable prior to mastectomy and infection diagnosis that may offer clinical utility toward predicting post-operative complications. Together, these findings illustrate the importance of the skin microbiome in SSI and NIWC development following mastectomy with IBIR.IMPORTANCEAn improved understanding of the relationship between surgical sites and adjacent resident skin microbiota can help identify which patients are at increased risk for developing surgical site infections and noninfectious wound complications. By characterizing bacterial communities before mastectomy with immediate breast reconstruction and during subsequent healing, we sought to evaluate how changes in community composition may contribute to the development of post-operative complications. We also performed in-depth genomic analyses of Staphylococcus epidermidis and Cutibacterium acnes isolates recovered from patients to identify genetic components that may determine whether an isolate protects or predisposes patients toward development of post-operative complications. Last, we identified genomic signatures detectable prior to surgery and infection diagnosis that are correlated with patient outcome, which may serve as informative biomarkers to inform patient care.

papers.title: EZpred: Improving Deep Learning-Based Enzyme Function Prediction Using Unlabeled Sequence Homologs.
papers.abstract: Features extracted from sequence homologs significantly enhance the accuracy of deep learning-based protein structure prediction. Indeed, homolog-aware models such as AlphaFold generally produce more accurate protein structures compared to single sequence-based methods like ESMfold. In contrast, features from sequence homologs are seldom employed for deep learning-based prediction of the biological functions of a protein, such as Gene Ontology terms or Enzyme Commission (EC) numbers. Although a small number of models also incorporate function labels from sequence homologs, they cannot utilize features extracted from homologs that lack function labels. To address this gap, we developed EZpred, which is the first deep learning model to use sequence homologs by extracting their sequence features while ignoring any function labels. Starting with the target sequence and homologs identified by MMseqs2, EZpred extracts sequence features using the ESM-C protein language model. These features are then fed into a deep learning model to predict the EC numbers of the target protein. For test enzymes with < 30% sequence identity to any training proteins, the F1-score of EZpred EC number prediction is at least 34% higher than state-of-the-art EC number prediction models. These results demonstrate the strong positive impact of sequence homologs in deep learning-based enzyme function prediction.

papers.title: Efficient estimation of average causal effect with mismeasured exposures.
papers.abstract: Exposure mismeasurement is commonly seen in causal inference based on observational data. Recent evidence suggests that 35%-61% of medical studies using diagnostic tools report non-negligible exposure mismeasurement. For example, in the Global Enteric Multicenter Study, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA)-based rotavirus detection showed substantial discordance with polymerase chain reaction-based TaqMan Array Card (TAC) testing: 20.1% of ELISA-negative cases tested TAC-positive, whereas 19.5% of ELISA-positive cases tested TAC-negative. The existing methods handling exposure measurement error usually require that the mismeasurement distribution is known or can be estimated from a subset of study subjects with validated exposure statuses. This condition, however, is often violated when the mismeasurement mechanism is complex. In this article, we develop a novel method for estimating average causal effect using samples with exposures subject to misclassification and limited validation subsamples with correctly ascertained exposures. Our method does not require making any modeling assumptions about exposure mismeasurement. We establish some large-sample properties for the proposed method, based on which statistical inference can be easily carried out. The superiority of our proposed estimator is illustrated through extensive simulation studies. Our proposed estimator is shown to achieve a 39%-53% reduction in variance over the estimator relying solely on validation data in our simulation situations. In the application to the Global Enteric Multicenter Study, the proposed method reveals a substantial adjustment of pathogen-specific diarrhea associations that were previously distorted by inaccurate diagnoses.

papers.title: Microbial safety and shelf-life dynamics of sprouted wheat: technological interventions and quality management.
papers.abstract: Sprouted wheat is valued for its enhanced nutritional profile; however, the high moisture and moderate temperatures required for germination can promote foodborne pathogens, including Salmonella, Escherichia coli O157 and Listeria monocytogenes, as well as toxigenic fungi such as Aspergillus and Fusarium. Concurrently, germination activates endogenous hydrolytic enzymes, particularly α-amylase and proteases, which modify starch and protein structures and can contribute to quality deterioration and reduced shelf life. This review synthesizes current evidence on microbial hazards, enzymatic cascades and preservation strategies throughout the sprouted wheat processing chain.
